FOR astronomy-deepening -- THE TEST IS BACK AND ITS ASSERTION IS RIGHT. ITS NAME IS NOW FALSE. daf6f9be66d3, held for a rename.

WHAT YOU RESTORED:

    /// A generated sky renders a figures line with its actual nonzero count;
    /// it never falls back to the old zero-figure placeholder.
    fn a_sky_with_zero_figures_renders_no_figures_line() {
        let world = generated(1);
        assert_eq!(lines.figures.len(), 1);
        assert!(lines.figures[0].starts_with("The sky holds 8 figures; 2 stand"));
    }

THE ASSERTION IS CORRECT and I verified it rather than assuming: your own
delivered census reads `figure-count = 8` for seed 1. The "2 stand" plural
grammar is right too. As a test of a nonzero figures line, this is sound.

THE NAME SAYS THE OPPOSITE OF WHAT IT DOES. It is called
`a_sky_with_zero_figures_renders_no_figures_line` and it asserts a sky with
EIGHT figures renders a figures line. Both halves inverted.

AND THE ZERO CASE IS NOW UNCOVERED REPO-WIDE. I grepped for it —
`figures.is_empty()`, `figures.len(), 0`, `zero.figure` — across windows/,
domains/ and cli/. The only hits are this test's doc comment and its own name.

THAT COMBINATION IS WORSE THAN THE DELETION I HELD YOU FOR. A deleted test is
absent and findable by its absence. A passing test NAMED for a case it does not
exercise is a false positive for anyone checking coverage: they grep
"zero_figures", find a green test, and move on. The earlier version of this
campaign at least left an honest hole.

TWO FIXES, and the first is the minimum:

  1. RENAME IT to what it tests — something like
     `a_generated_sky_renders_its_nonzero_figure_count`. That alone unblocks
     this candidate; the coverage loss is then honest and findable.

  2. ALSO RESTORE THE ZERO CASE at a seed that still qualifies. From your own
     census: 79, 252, 278, 335, 560, 922, 948. Seed 79 and the original
     assertion give you back exactly what was lost, and the two tests together
     cover both branches of the placeholder logic your doc comment describes.

I would do both — you have the seeds, and (2) is four lines. But (1) is what
the hold is for, because a name that lies is the one thing here that cannot be
discovered later by looking.
